#27. How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1430 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1430 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people’s lives.
  • Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts.
  • According to recent reports, A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people’s lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities.

Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people’s impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences.

According to recent reports, A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity.

Recent findings suggest that fire doesn’t just happen anywhere. Although plenty of flammable materials exist in natural settings, not every place experiences wildfires. Some prairies burn almost every year, while many forests go without major fires for hundreds of years. Researchers explain these differences in terms of fire regimes, which are patterns describing when, how often, and how widely and intensely fires occur.

Sources indicate that weather is a major factor affecting fire regimes. An abundance of rain helps grow grass and trees that can become fuel for fires. Whether they do or not, however, can depend on the moisture inside plants; plants with enough moisture do not burn easily. By contrast, dry conditions make them more likely to catch fire. When a drought lasts, vegetation becomes increasingly flammable. Strong winds also accelerate fire growth and spread enormously.

Human activity often combines with weather conditions to cause fires. Even routine outdoor recreation can accidentally start a fire. More people venture outdoors during sunny, drier times of the year, increasing the risk of accidental fires when dry vegetation is more likely to be present.

Industry observers note that the double-sided role of humans in fire also adds to the difficulty. Humans do start fires, but they also put them out. Firefighters contain fires that could have gone worse if no action had been taken and can keep them from spreading. Humans can also take preventative actions, such as clearing flammable material.

Sources indicate that sometimes the line between starting fires and preventing them becomes blurred. One way to clear out flammable material is to intentionally set fires to make future fires more manageable. However, these fires are hard to distinguish from other fires through satellite monitoring.

Sources indicate that an experiment is one way to find out how humans affect wildfires. If everyone stayed home under the same weather, their impact on fires would be revealed. This is why Wang’s research team focused on the COVID-19 era. It was what’s called a “natural experiment,” in which experimental conditions arose without any action by researchers.

Wang explained: “Human activity and climate normally vary together, because seasons, farming calendars, and weather all shape both fire and human behavior. The early-2020 lockdowns produced an abrupt, large-scale drop in human mobility, and the timing differed across countries while the weather did not change in the same way. This gave us a natural experiment.”.

The researchers defined the period of restricted mobility by checking regional lockdown orders and mobile phone location data. Data from NASA and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Suomi NPP satellite helped the team track fires. Its VIIRS sensor detects heat signatures from fires at a spatial resolution of 375 meters. Each hot spot the satellite detects counts as an active-fire detection, meaning one large fire can appear as multiple spots. However, the satellite records both wildfires and prescribed burns without distinguishing between them. As a result, the intent behind each fire remains unknown.

Recent findings suggest that in the study, detections during the 2020 restriction periods were compared with those from the same weeks in 2013–2019. Weather conditions weren’t exactly the same as in past years, which was accounted for.

Industry observers note that the results show that areas under lockdown in the first half of 2020 had about 12.3 percent fewer active-fire detections than the recent-past average. The drop varied by vegetation type. In forests, fires decreased by about 27.7 percent, while grasslands decreased by 8.4 percent. Shrublands, savannas, and croplands didn’t show much difference. The researchers interpret this to mean that humans are a major cause of fires in forests and grasslands.

Controlling for weather factors was key in the study. Without adjustments, the drop was only 5.8 percent, which was not statistically significant. After controlling for weather, however, the estimated decline increased to 12.3 percent. If weather in 2020 were more favorable to fires than in previous years, it might have masked some of the human impact.

Sources indicate that the 12.3 percent decrease in fire detections doesn’t mean that humans directly caused this share of fires. Restricting human activity shrank both humans’ impact on starting fires and likely limited their impact on extinguishing them. The 12.3 percent figure is the net effect after these two opposing forces partly cancel out.

Wang mentioned, “The 12.3 percent is a net effect, not the share of fires caused by humans; opposing changes in ignition and suppression mean it does not capture the full magnitude of human influence.”.

In regional data, some areas experienced a considerable increase in fire after human mobility was restricted. Most of South America, southern Africa, and northeast Asia saw an increase in fire during the COVID-19 lockdowns. Notable increases include 31.4 percent in Colombia, 25.4 percent in India, and 70.7 percent in Honduras.

It has been revealed that there are no direct field data showing why this occurred. The researchers inferred that diminished fire suppression capacity resulted in more fires in these locations, but Wang acknowledged, “It is an inference, not a direct observation.” That inference was based in part on earlier studies that suggested that weaker fire management in Colombia and Madagascar contributed to increased fires.

One line of evidence is how fires reacted to different levels of mobility loss, based on fire counts in 0.5-degree grid cells. In countries with fewer fires, fire declined in almost a straight line as mobility decreased. But countries that experienced more fires showed a slow increase that leveled off at about 27 percent on average as mobility fell. The researchers interpreted this as a sign that different mechanisms were at work. The steady decline fits fewer human-driven ignitions, while the gradual rise points to weakened suppression. But Wang mentioned that there could be other reasons, such as changes in local land use.

According to recent reports, mobility restrictions may also have disrupted fire management activities, which could mean that fewer fires were set for management purposes. The researchers examined 12 countries with records of prescribed burning. The area burned by prescribed fires in 2020 decreased by about half compared to the 2013–2019 average. Of course, the locations and sizes of prescribed burns also shift from year to year with fire return intervals and land-management cycles, which complicates this analysis.

When areas subjected to prescribed burning were excluded in those 12 countries, the decline in fires there shrank from 45.3 percent to 27.8 percent.

This research has limits partly because it relied on mobile phone data to track human movement. This kind of data might not capture human activity in rural areas where coverage may be limited. Also, the analysis focused only on the first half of each year, so the impact on regions where fires happen more frequently in the latter half of the year, such as the western US, may not have been fully captured.

Wang explained that this quasi-experimental design provides strong associational evidence but is not a controlled experiment.

Sources indicate that wang emphasized that the study is not an evaluation of fire policies. The analysis does, however, suggest that there’s no single ideal policy response. Where fires decreased, human ignition seems to dominate. In those areas, reducing accidental ignitions through public education and maintaining beneficial prescribed burning can be key. On the other hand, areas where fires increased might need to address reduced monitoring and suppression. Maintaining firefighting and patrol capacity during disruptions can be important there.

Sources indicate that wang added, “Overall, a uniform policy is unlikely to work, and strategies should be tailored to local human-fire relationships.” Fire-risk projections might benefit from accounting for human behavior. That way, more accurate fire projections can be made even as weather and society change.

Industry observers note that cell Reports Sustainability, 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.crsus.2026.100860.

#25. How to clear the application cache on your Mac

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (597 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

How to clear the application cache on your Mac

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (597 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Clearing app caches don’t necessarily make your Mac run faster.
  • Your Mac applications often store temporary files, called caches, to improve user experience.
  • Recent findings suggest that for example, Google Chrome builds its app cache as you visit different websites.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clearing app caches don’t necessarily make your Mac run faster.

Your Mac applications often store temporary files, called caches, to improve user experience. This is a recommended best practice that most developers follow to prevent apps from creating or redownloading the same files each time you use them. App caches include temporary files like image previews, downloaded content and other data that help apps launch quickly and serve content without additional processing.

Recent findings suggest that for example, Google Chrome builds its app cache as you visit different websites. It caches parts of webpages, like images, which helps speed up load times when you visit the same website next time. However, the problem with leaving application caches unchecked is that it could continue taking up storage space even when an application no longer requires the cached files.

Although your Mac may manage these temporary files, there's no guarantee when this process occurs. Moreover, problematic app caches can contribute to glitches, like displaying outdated or inaccurate content. Knowing how to clear app caches on your Mac can help resolve complications arising from an outdated cache or reclaim storage space wasted on bloating caches.

Recent findings suggest that some Mac applications allow clearing app caches from within the app itself. For example, Safari and Apple Music include the options to clear app caches in their settings menu. However, this is not the case for every Mac app out there; you'll need to manually find their caches to delete them.

Your Mac typically stores application caches in ~/library/caches. Since the library is treated as a hidden directory, your Mac may not readily reveal it in the Finder. To view the library folder: Finder > command + shift + H > command + J > check "show Library Folder." Once in the library folder, press command + J > check "Calculate all sizes" to display folder sizes alongside folder names.

In the caches folder, look for the application cache you want to clear. You can distinguish third-party apps from first-party Apple apps from the folder names and prefixes. First-party Apple apps use the "com.apple" prefix in their bundle identifier, while third-party apps don't. Open the application folder in question and delete everything inside to clear its app cache. If an app cache doesn't exist in the caches folder, you can look for it in ~/library/containers. The containers folder includes apps that run in a sandbox, so their cache is also isolated. Whether your app caches are in caches or containers, you'll need to apply the same principle for finding and deleting them.

Sources indicate that it's worth understanding that clearing app caches doesn't necessarily improve application performance unless your Mac is already running short on storage space. However, deleting app caches can help reclaim storage space and sometimes even resolve app glitches. When you launch an app after clearing its cache, you might notice the app taking longer to launch, and using it might feel sluggish. This happens because the app has to rebuild its cache all over again. However, once this process is complete, your app should feel smooth and snappy to use.

It is not recommended to indiscriminately clear app caches or build a maintenance routine that involves one. Your Mac apps rely on caches to ensure a smooth user experience. You should only ever clear app caches if you notice the app not behaving as expected or if an app is taking up too much storage space. Otherwise, it's best to leave app caches alone and let your Mac manage it at its discretion.

Digital photo frames aren't new technology, but they're still one of my favorite pieces of tech to put into a home. These devices promise something simple: a beautiful frame to display all the photos sitting on your camera roll, displayed for you to enjoy at any time.

Industry observers note that best of all, you don't have to settle for just a digital photo frame anymore. Want something that doubles as a family calendar or has a voice assistant to answer your questions? This guide has picks for that. Want something totally wireless? I've tested those, too.

In a recent development, I've been testing digital photo frames for almost six years now and always sing their praises. These devices are designed to look like a regular photo frame, but with a screen inside that displays whichever photos you send to it. There's always an app involved to upload images, and you can also usually send photos over email, too. Both the email option and the app let you invite other family members to the frame, so multiple people can send images. It's perfect for families living in the same house or for long-distance family members who want to share their best pictures with Grandma.

It has been revealed that I also like that these devices are fairly intuitive and minimal. Digital photo frames simply connect to your Wi-Fi and display your photos. There are also options that can do multiple things if you want a multipurpose device in your home, but your frame doesn't have to do anything but show your photos.

In a recent development, do you have any photos on a digital device, like a smartphone, computer, or camera? Or does someone in your family have photos they could send to you or directly to the frame itself? Then yes, a digital photo frame is absolutely worth buying. If you have photos you take and want to see regularly or wish you had all your wedding photos on display instead of just the ones that fit on your wall, a digital photo frame will easily solve that for you.

In a recent development, they're also great to purchase as a gift. I've given two different digital photo frames to my parents over the years and am currently helping my mother pick one out to gift my grandmother to enjoy photos in her nursing home. It's a great gift for young parents, too, who have camera rolls packed with photos of their new baby (or their fur baby!) and photo aficionados who will never have enough frames in their house for their work.

There's no beating Aura when it comes to digital frames, and it's the option I recommend most to everyone in my life after using Aura's frames since 2021. All of them have high-quality displays and unlimited photo storage, a combo you won't find anywhere else. Aura's frames are simple to set up, use, and share with family and friends, too. Everything is controlled with the app, so there's no laggy touchscreen to futz with—you can scroll through or heart photos using the touch bar on top and use the app to control how quickly your photos change and other settings. My frames are shared with my husband, but I can also scroll down and see my parents’ frames that they've shared with me, all in one application.

Aura has had a lot of frame designs over the years, but it’s focused now on its mat-style frames that look fantastic in your home. These frames all have different names, but are nearly identical otherwise. The 10-inch Carver Mat ($179) is a mat version of the popular affordable Carver frame, and it sits in a landscape mode that will show vertical photos side by side. The other two are the 12-inch Aspen ($229) and 15-inch Walden ($299), which are flat on the back so that they can be mounted on a wall in either landscape or portrait mode. I've tried all three, and my personal favorite is the Walden for my home, but that's since I have one massive great room that encompasses the dining room, kitchen, and living room, and the Walden sits in a far corner but is easily visible from any point in the room. If you're working with a more normal room size, the Carver and Aspen are both great sizes, but I do like that the Aspen can be rotated to portrait or landscape orientation; the Carver will only do landscape, and can't be wall-mounted, either. It's up to you if that's worth spending more.

No matter which model you choose, the best part about the Aura frames is that they don't look like shiny computer screens nor are they haunted by the blue tinge you'll find on cheaper digital frames. Especially thanks to the mat style you'll find on these three models, they can easily pass for a real photo—until the picture changes, of course. There's really no better experience you can find in the world of digital photo frames.

Industry observers note that I've liked Skylight's photo frames well enough, but my favorite product from Skylight is its digital wall calendars. These calendars double as digital photo frames and digital wall calendars since you can set up a photo screensaver to pop up when you aren't interacting with it. The only downside is you'll have to pay a subscription fee to use the photo feature, but all of Skylight's devices have some kind of paywall associated with them.

According to recent reports, the Skylight Calendar 2 is the newest of its three calendar models, but feels like the Goldilocks option with its 15-inch screen that's a good size for kitchen countertops or to mount on the wall, faster performance compared to older models, a more reasonable price point (the Skylight Calendar Max has a wild price tag), and interchangeable snap frames so you can adjust the look of your device to match your current home aesthetic. It's a great device that has made it easy to peek at my family's calendar whenever I want, and my son uses the Skylight Buddy in his room to track his own daily routine, but I could also teach him to just use the Calendar 2 for it instead. While the screen isn't as matte as the Aura frames, photos still look great on this screen, and the uploader tool is easy to use.

If you like the idea of Skylight but don't want a subscription to have the photo feature (and don't mind missing out on the calendar and chores), you can get the Skylight Frame 2 ($190). There's still a subscription option for that model for certain features, like making albums and having a cloud backup, but you don't need it to have the basic digital photo frame experience. The Frame-only subscription is cheaper than the calendar one—$39 a year for Frame Plus versus $79 a year for Calendar Plus—but you get less, since the Calendar Plus subscription includes meal planning, an AI uploading tool, and more. I like Skylight's options a lot, especially with the latest calendar-based ecosystem, but the subscription fee is the main downside. But you can get a lot more features out of your device.

I didn't expect to like Amazon's newly introduced Alexa Photo Frame. I thought it would be gimmicky and frustrating to use, especially as someone who's hated Amazon's photo uploader tool in the past for its smart displays. But I found myself surprisingly pleased not only with the frame itself, but even the smart speaker experience built into it. It does help that I already have an Amazon Prime subscription, which you'll want to have unlimited photo storage and to get Alexa+ voice access on the device.

Recent findings suggest that what helps is that the Alexa Photo Frame uses the Amazon Photos app. It's similar to the Google Photos app in that it wants to back up all your photos for you from your phone, and it also connects to and controls this new digital photo frame. (I can also control which photos are added to my other Alexa smart displays through the app under the devices tab, so it's not exclusive to the Alexa Photo Frame.) I uploaded a handful of photos to the frame and was impressed with how nice the experience looked. The display looked a little more matte than my Skylight Calendar 2 when I put them side by side, and it has a mat-style frame that reminds me of the Aura frames. The Alexa Photo Frame has only a 10.1-inch screen, and no option to rotate it between landscape or portrait; the included stand puts it into landscape mode only, making it much like the Aura Carver Mat in specs and design. It does not, however, have a Photo Match option, so the paired vertical photos can look a bit random.

The Alexa Photo Frame also costs more than the Carver, since it comes with an extra bonus: Amazon's AI-powered voice assistant, Alexa+. I was impressed that even though this device is flat enough to be wall-mounted, Alexa's voice still sounded full and clear without any tinny quality, and music actually sounded pretty good too. I'd prefer a real speaker, but if you wanted one device for just photos and simple questions without any other screen clutter, this is a good option. This device is best for Prime users who will get Alexa+ for free and free photo storage to boot.

Sources indicate that aura came out with the first Aura Ink frame last fall, and I was impressed by its unique color E Ink screen and fully wireless experience that made it a frame I was actually willing to mount on my wall. As of this week, Aura has a upcoming addition to its cordless Ink lineup: the Ink 10-inch, which has a smaller screen, expanded color palette, and 200 pixels-per-inch resolution.

Like the Aura frames I recommend throughout this story, the Aura Ink 10-inch has unlimited storage and is run through Aura's clean, intuitive app that has no subscription tiers. But the Ink 10-inch (and the larger Ink 13-inch) use an E Ink screen like a color e-reader does to run on a battery, so you can place the frame anywhere without needing to constantly plug it in. While the Ink 10-inch is smaller, it has a new nine-color e-paper display that adds off-white, mustard yellow, and orange to its color wheel. It still has a newspaper-like look to it, and Aura's technology will run photos through its algorithm to convert them onto the e-paper screen.

The Aura Ink defaults to only show one photo a day to preserve battery life and because the transition to change photos takes longer than on a standard screen. But the Ink 10-inch does have a prettier, melt-like transition effect instead of the flashing that the Ink 13-inch does when it switches photos overnight. There's also a subtle front light in both the Ink 10-inch and Ink 13-inch, but it looks best when hit with natural light to help illuminate it. It's a great option if you want something that won't have a cord and don't mind a newspaper-like look. It looks more realistic than other frames with this e-paper screen; friends of mine have genuinely been shocked when I tell them it's a digital frame.

Recent findings suggest that the Aura Carver has been around for a while, and it's still a great frame. The 10-inch frame is one of the best cheap frames you can find, pairing Aura's fantastic experience (a great app! unlimited storage!) with a smaller, landscape-only option. While it does have a slimmer aspect ratio of 16:10, landscape photos still look good, and you can toggle on Photo Match in the settings to have the frame “match” to similar portrait orientation photos together to fill the screen. It'll often match by event or match two photos of the same person together.

The Aura Carver also has the Carver Mat ($179) version for a little higher price tag that matches the aesthetic of the other mat versions and is included as part of our top pick. But if you're looking for the cheapest option while still getting the great experience Aura offers, the base Aura Carver is the cheapest you'll find. It's also often on sale during events like Black Friday, so keep an eye out.

Nixplay Classic 10.1-Inch Frame for $190: Nixplay is semi-comparable to Aura, with a range of digital photo frames that's been around for years. But you will be hit with a subscription fee if you want more than 500 MB of photos on your device—Nixplay Lite costs $20 a year for 100 GB, while Nixplay Plus costs $30 for unlimited photo storage. You'll get other features, too, like ability to add longer video clips and connect to more frames, but the storage aspect is the part you'll run into after using this frame for a long time. I tested the Classic 10.1" Frame that's been around for a while, and while it's easy and intuitive to use, I found the settings slow to update from changes I make in the app, and I don't like the distracting transitions the frame will use by default. It also has a surprising amount of border for vertical photos in portrait mode. It's still a fine frame overall, especially if you're able to manage your storage usage, but it remains only an honorable mention for me still. Plus, you can get the Aura Carver for cheaper for the same size screen and unlimited storage (but you won't get a touchscreen or ability to rotate between portrait and landscape modes, which the Nixplay Classic can do).

Industry observers note that skylight Frame 2 for $190: Skylight's photo frames are where the company originated, but I do prefer its calendars over its photo frames. The Frame 2 is its latest generation, and the best part is that you can swap out the frames, which Skylight named Snap Frames (starting at $15), to match the style of your home. You can upload photos by app or email, but you will need a subscription—Frame Plus, which costs $39 a year—to create albums, adjust settings using the app, upload videos, and add captions. The subscription doesn't control your actual storage, and instead the Frame 2 has a limit of 16 GB of storage.

Aura Mason for $199: The major original favorite from Aura, with a solid frame and the ability to rotate between landscape and portrait mode. It's still a great frame, but Aura did say they're sunsetting the model, but it'll remain available until it's sold out. It's still available so far.

Azorpa 10-Inch Digital Photo Frame for $90: This slim frame works well and has a nice affordable price point, and it can be rotated. It also has its own dedicated app, unlike several affordable models that all use the same Frameo app. But the ratio is slimmer than smartphone photos, so I found myself needing to constantly recrop pictures or have an extra border along two of the sides. If you don't mind a border and want a really cheap frame, this one's solid.

Recent findings suggest that cozyla frames: Our staffers have tried a few digital photo frames from this brand, and one of its digital wall calendars. Photo quality was great and there were solid features like only showing photos that match the current orientation of the frame. Our reviewer found the app to be frustrating, however, and it comes preloaded with unnecessary art images.

Familink 10-Inch Digital Photo Frame for $200: Familink's frame works with or without an internet connection, thanks to its 4G SIM card. Someone will need to set up an account on the website or app (iOS, Android) so that family members can send photos (or even chats) to the frame. There was no slideshow feature when we tested it in 2024, but the screen still looked good.

Sources indicate that loop Family Frame for $200: This is a good option if you want to text photos to a display, instead of using an app or an email. It's a good convenient option to use with family members. It's a solid overall photo frame, and has a touchscreen.

It has been revealed that pexar 2K Digital Picture Frame by Lexar for $180: This frame can rotate to be either portrait or landscape mode, and has a little stand that attaches via magnet for either position. It's a fine frame, but the screen isn't as nice as those for a similar price. The Pexar is made by Lexar but uses a third-party app, Frameo, which works fine but has a weirdly Instagram-like uploader that's limited to 10 photos.

Skylight 10-Inch Frame for $190: A previous honorable mention, this frame is still solid. We like other frames better for the price, including the upcoming Skylight Frame 2 (especially with its Snap Frame accessories). There's both a 10-inch version (with only 8 GB of storage) and a 15-inch version (with 16 GB of storage).

Sources indicate that vieunite's Textura Digital Canvas for $754 (USD shown in cart): Beautiful for displaying professional art, this one is bright and high-def enough that you don't lose the integrity of the original painting. It's extremely expensive, though, even if it's cheaper than buying an actual van Gogh.

How Do Digital Photo Frames Work?

Digital photo frames collect your photos, usually through an app but also through email and sometimes text, and display them onto the digital screen. They're created to look like a real frame, but instead show off hundreds or thousands of photos without you needing to reframe anything or print every single picture. Our favorite picks all have an app with storage, so they use Wi-Fi to connect the photos to the frame, but some frames also have physical storage on the device to store and remember the pictures.

What Should You Look For In a Digital Photo Frame?

Here are the top features you should check in a frame:.

What Storage Options Are There on Digital Photo Frames?

Sources indicate that all the main frames we recommend use cloud-based storage, so you'll upload your photos to a cloud server for the frame to reach and display them. Aura has unlimited storage for photos, while Nixplay charges $30 a year for unlimited photo storage (along with other features). While both use cloud storage, these are both reputable companies with defined privacy and security practices. Some of the cheaper frames you'll find won't have these processes in place.

Some frames have internal storage that can be expanded with SD cards or even use a USB stick. These options can be more secure, especially if you're moving photos yourself from the computer to the USB or SD card and then connecting it to the frame, but it’s also more work.

Do Smart Displays Work as Digital Photo Frames?

Sources indicate that if you already have a smart display, you can set it to cycle through your photo albums when it's idle. The best one for this by far is the Google Nest Max ($230), though the Apple HomeView is another option I'm considering for this guide. It uses Google Photos to pull pictures, so if you're already a Google Photos user, it's an easy transition. But even if you aren't, adding your pictures to Google Photos is much, much easier than using Amazon's uploading tool in the Alexa app if you're using an Echo Show display, though you can also use the Amazon Photos app that works similar to the Google Photos app. You'll use that app for the Alexa Photo Frame I recommend above.

How Does Privacy and Security Come Into Play With Digital Photo Frames?

It has been revealed that you might not think that photos count as sensitive information, compared to a bank account statement or your Social Security number. But it can be devastating to find photos of loved ones used for nefarious or unsavory purposes.

This is why we prefer frames from reputable companies like Aura and Nixplay over cheaper ones with less clearly defined privacy and security practices. Nixplay offers reasonable security measures, like encrypting your photos during transmission, and Aura offers the option to delete metadata, like the location where a photo was captured. However, both say they may disclose personal information if court-ordered or subpoenaed, and neither provides safety guarantees against hacking.

If you're concerned about security, you can avoid connecting to third-party services, but your most secure option is to just download several photos on a tablet and disable all internet connectivity.

Amid the Jensen Huang fallout, Maria Cantwell accuses Howard Lutnick of giving away ‘America’s technology advantage in AI.’﻿.

Washington Senator Maria Cantwell, one of the top Democrats on the Senate commerce committee, has taken fire at the Department of Commerce (DOC) under Secretary Howard Lutnick for neglecting to enforce protections intended to keep Nvidia’s AI chips away from China. In a letter to Lutnick on Sunday, Cantwell noted the DOC has “undermined America’s national security,” and that its failures “help give away America’s technology advantage in AI.”.

Industry observers note that “Despite clear authority from Congress, the Department of Commerce has allowed advanced AI chips to flow through companies with ties to the People’s Republic of China (PRC). The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology.”.

In her letter, Cantwell specifically calls out instances when the DOC reportedly didn’t heed warnings from White House and intelligence officials to restrict Megaspeed’s access to AI chips, prior to allegations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a then-Megaspeed executive suspected of being a Chinese spy. Cantwell also criticizes the DOC for allowing Alibaba and ByteDance to access Nvidia chips through overseas data centers, and extending a loophole that let restricted companies obtain American AI technology through subsidiaries.

The DOC is also accused of “putting business interests ahead of national security,” with Cantwell noting that Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm formerly led by Lutnick and now steered by his sons, reportedly held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of Lutnick’s nomination for Commerce Secretary.

Sources indicate that the letter comes ahead of a meeting in China this Thursday between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. While Congress is looking to bolster export restrictions around AI chips, The Wall Street Journal reports that Lutnick is instead expected to unveil a fresh initiative that will designate Nvidia — along with companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon, and Microsoft — as an AI “national champion.” The designation reportedly aims to help these companies expand overseas and compete with Chinese technology firms by granting them expedited export licence approvals.

Industry observers note that “America cannot maintain its leadership in AI if the agency responsible for protecting that advantage fails to enforce its own controls,” Cantwell said, closing her letter. “The Administration must account for its failure to enforce these protections and take immediate action to prevent America’s most sensitive technology from strengthening our adversaries.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dreamteam, a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge.

Industry observers note that the funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest. The San Francisco-based startup declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation.

Sources indicate that traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date. That often leaves businesses with incomplete or outdated information. Dreamteam aims to eliminate much of that work by automatically capturing context from sources including emails and customer conversations. It also uses AI agents to handle tasks such as follow-ups, meeting preparation, and pipeline monitoring.

Dreamteam co-founder and CEO Anand Venkatraman (pictured above, right) told TechCrunch that he had repeatedly encountered problems with traditional CRM platforms over more than 25 years in enterprise software, including at Salesforce and Freshworks. Salespeople spent considerable time updating records, yet managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their business. “In all these years, I have never come across an instance where I could click a button and get a forecast from the CRM,” he said.

That experience led Venkatraman to co-found Dreamteam in 2025 with Senthil Kanthaswamy (pictured above, center), who spent more than nine years at Freshworks, most recently as a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy (pictured above, left), who previously worked on AI and platform engineering at Freshworks.

Sources indicate that at the heart of Dreamteam’s CRM is what it calls the Firm Brain. This acts as virtual memory, pulling together information from emails, meetings, and other customer interactions to build a shared record of customer relationships. Four built-in AI agents use that information to research prospects, draft follow-up emails, flag potential risks to deals, and configure CRM workflows, with sales teams retaining control over what gets sent to customers.

Dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling its product, with most paying for the service, Venkatraman said. The startup has also replaced established CRM platforms at several businesses, including Salesforce at healthcare manufacturer DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers.

The advertising sales team at media streaming company Plex also chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM alternatives, Venkatraman told TechCrunch. Plex’s co-founder and chief product officer Scott Olechowski mentioned Dreamteam’s ability to integrate with AI tools already used across the company was a “game changer.”.

According to recent reports, replacing established CRM platforms at scale may prove more difficult. In a blog post earlier this year, venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) argued that while AI could transform how businesses manage customer relationships, existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a new generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them.

Venkatraman acknowledged that Salesforce and HubSpot are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but noted that their entrenched positions do not guarantee they will dominate the next generation of CRM software.

“We see this as an electric-car moment for systems of record,” he remarked, adding that AI requires a fundamental rethink of how CRMs are built — not simply adding new features to existing platforms.

Kanthaswamy believes startups have a window of two to five years to gain ground before established CRM providers can fully adapt to AI. Rebuilding software around a fundamentally different architecture takes time, he stated, giving newer companies an opportunity to attract customers while incumbents work to overhaul their existing products.

Sources indicate that dreamteam also plans to expand beyond sales into other parts of the customer lifecycle, including onboarding, customer support, and upselling. The startup already has a feature called Magic Apps that allows consumers to create custom applications and dashboards within the CRM using natural-language instructions, without writing code.

Currently, Dreamteam employs more than 35 people, with its engineering team based in Chennai and its go-to-market operations in the United States. Kanthaswamy mentioned the startup aims to reach eight figures in annual revenue by the end of 2027, though he declined to disclose the startup’s current revenue.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple has debuted a research study and an iPhone app to learn how people use AI for health questions. The company confirmed the Apple Health AI Usage Study on Sunday. It runs in the US with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform that healthcare professionals use.

The study will look at what makes people trust health AI and how good its answers are, Apple mentioned. It will also measure how well people understand the answers and what they do next. Apple wants the findings to shape how it and the wider industry design health AI tools.

“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” remarked Sumbul Desai, Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness.

In a recent development, participants ask the study app everyday health questions. The answers use plain language and come with linked, peer-reviewed clinical citations. OpenEvidence draws on sources such as The New England Journal of Medicine, the Journal of the American Medical Association and Nature.

Participants can also choose to share HealthKit data, such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep or lab results. Apple wants to see whether that personal data makes the answers more relevant and easier to understand. The study will also test whether the app helps people prepare for visits with their own doctors.

The App Store lists it as the Apple Health AI Study App. Its listing adds two more uses: putting personal health data in context, and building a personalised exercise or meal proposal.

It has been revealed that consumer health tools built on large language models can give incomplete or unclear answers, Apple stated. That is why it wants research on how to present health information more clearly.

In a recent development, apple noted it will not use study data to train AI models. Participants decide whether to share any HealthKit data or survey answers. The app has guardrails meant to detect certain concerning questions and suggest that the participant follows up with a provider.

It has been revealed that apple has not integrated the app with Siri or Apple Intelligence, Steve Dent reported for Engadget. Its App Store listing indicates that neither the app nor the study provides medical advice, diagnosis or treatment.

“Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds,” mentioned Robert Wachter, who chairs UCSF’s Department of Medicine, in Apple’s announcement.

According to recent reports, the study is open to up to 200,000 people aged 21 or older in the US. They need an iPhone 15 Pro or later running iOS 26 or later, the models that support Apple Intelligence.

According to recent reports, openEvidence teamed up with Anthropic in September to offer free medical AI to doctors. OpenAI introduced ChatGPT Health in January, and Microsoft and Perplexity followed in March with Copilot Health and Perplexity Health.

Breaking: ULA Vulcan rocket failure destroys 40 Amazon Leo satellites

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (580 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s the alliance's first launch failure since it formed in 2006.
  • According to recent reports, united Launch Alliance is known for its ultra-dependable Atlas V, but its its latest rocket is off to a sputtering start.
  • "Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," the organization said in a post on X.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s the alliance's first launch failure since it formed in 2006.

According to recent reports, united Launch Alliance is known for its ultra-dependable Atlas V, but its its latest rocket is off to a sputtering start. The fresh heavy-lift Vulcan rocket malfunctioned while climbing into space yesterday, destroying its payload of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites.

"Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," the organization said in a post on X. "We will work closely with our customer and other appropriate organizations to find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as swiftly as possible.".

Industry observers note that launch failures are always a risk, but amazingly, United Launch Alliance had never experienced one previously. Since the organization formed in 2006 as a partnership between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, its Atlas V rocket has been famously dependable. Now, the company's more powerful, more complex Vulcan will be under review by engineers and is facing a possible grounding.

Industry observers note that "Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don't have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today," United Launch Alliance wrote. "ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action.".

In a recent development, following a refuelling problem that scrubbed a Friday launch, it was eventually rescheduled for Sunday, November 15th at around noon ET. However, controllers called a hold at T-minus 20 seconds due to an unknown technical issue. The problem was resolved before the end of the launch window and the rocket roared off the pad at 12:40 PM ET.

In a recent development, the solid boosters, which caused problems on two earlier flights, appeared to work normally. However, the first-stage methane engines fired longer than expected based on ULA's estimated timeline, as Spaceflight Now pointed out. After the first stage separated, the hydrogen-powered Centaur upper stage engines came on line for a planned 12.25-minute burn. The anomaly apparently occurred during that phase, ULA remarked on its website.

It has been revealed that as well as being a major setback for United Launch Alliance, the failed launch will be a blow to Amazon's Leo internet satellite system, intended to rival SpaceXSI's Starlink network. Leo has 38 Vulcan flights booked to launch its satellites, following eight successful Atlas V missions. Many of those are now likely to be delayed.

Amazon's other launch provider, Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin, suffered its own setback in May when its New Glenn rocket exploded on the launchpad. The company has 24 flights booked on that rocket.

The Federal Communications Commission required Amazon Leo to have 1,600 satellites in orbit by July 31, 2026, but so far it only has around 390 in service. The tech giant still planned to have 3,232 satellites in orbit by July 2029, but that goal may now be harder to obtain. "No operator could have predicted that all three core heavy-lift launch programs... would experience repeated, concurrent scheduling slips severe enough to exhaust the buffers Amazon Leo had built in," the company said back in July. With the failure of ULA's Vulcan on top of those delays, Leo can't seem to buy a break.

Latest Update: Make iOS 27 Less Glassy and Siri Less Clingy With These Settings

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that liquid Glass, Apple’s translucent design language, is front and center in iOS 27, with menus and controls that let your wallpaper and app content show through.
  • Recent findings suggest that that’s one of five iOS 27 defaults worth revisiting, along with how long Siri keeps your conversations, whether those conversations sync across devices, when subtitles appear on videos and how much Siri learns from individual apps.
  • Read more: Win a New Apple Watch in CNET Massive Guessing Game Contest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that liquid Glass, Apple’s translucent design language, is front and center in iOS 27, with menus and controls that let your wallpaper and app content show through. If the see-through look makes text harder to read or simply isn’t your taste, a setting in Display & Brightness can tone it down further for you.

Recent findings suggest that that’s one of five iOS 27 defaults worth revisiting, along with how long Siri keeps your conversations, whether those conversations sync across devices, when subtitles appear on videos and how much Siri learns from individual apps. Each one takes a few taps to change, but it isn’t too difficult to do so. We’ve outlined how to do so in this article.

Read more: Win a New Apple Watch in CNET Massive Guessing Game Contest.

Apple introduced Liquid Glass with iOS 26, giving menus, buttons, notifications and other interface elements a translucent appearance. Not everyone was a fan of the upcoming design, and with iOS 27, you now get more control over exactly how transparent the interface looks.

In a recent development, go to Settings > Appearance > Liquid Glass. Drag the slider to the right to add more tint and opacity, making buttons and text easier to distinguish from whatever is behind them. Moving it left makes the interface more transparent.

Recent findings suggest that if the most opaque setting still isn’t enough, go to Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size and turn on Reduce Transparency. This makes translucent backgrounds more solid across iOS, although it overrides the regular Liquid Glass appearance controls.

More tint makes Liquid Glass easier to read.

The fresh Siri AI works similarly t ChatGPT or Claude in iOS 27. It now comes complete with a dedicated app where you can revisit previous conversations. Those chats sync through iCloud so you can start a conversation on your iPhone and continue it on another Apple device, such as your Mac.

By default, iOS 27 keeps those conversations forever, but there is a way to automatically get rid of older conversations if you don’t want them piling up.

It has been revealed that if you don’t need a permanent archive of everything you ask Siri, go to Settings > Siri > Keep Conversations and choose 30 Days or 1 Year. Selecting either option permanently deletes conversations beyond that timeframe.

Siri keeps your conversations forever unless you choose a shorter limit.

While you’re there, tap Opens To and select A Fresh Conversation if you want the Siri app to open with a blank chat instead of showing your recent conversations every time.

Siri AI requires an iPhone 15 Pro or 15 Pro Max, iPhone Air or an iPhone 16 or later.

According to recent reports, iOS 27 puts a new Write with Siri button above the keyboard in apps including Messages, Mail and Notes. You can ask Siri AI to draft something from scratch, proofread what you’ve written or rewrite it in a different tone.

The thing is, I’m not a significant fan of the AI writing tools, so I don’t use them at all.

In a recent development, if you prefer writing without the extra AI prompt like I do, you can restrict Siri’s writing features by using Screen Time. Go to Settings > Screen Time > Content & Privacy Restrictions, turn on the restriction and then tap Siri > Writing Assistance > Don’t Allow.

Screen Time lets you completely disable Siri’s writing tools.

In a recent development, this disables access to the writing tools across your iPhone, rather than simply hiding the keyboard button, so only do this if you don’t use Apple’s AI writing tools at all. You can return to the same menu and choose Allow if you want them back. Apple documents the restriction under its Apple Intelligence Screen Time controls.

Introduced back in iOS 17, Siri can now wake up when you simply say “Siri” instead of “Hey Siri.” The one-word command is convenient, but it also makes accidental activations more likely whenever someone indicates Siri’s name in a conversation or a video they’re watching online.

Siri goes absolutely bonkers whenever I’m in work meetings about Apple features.

Recent findings suggest that to disable the feature, go to Settings > Siri > Talk to Siri. Choose “Hey Siri” instead of “Siri.”.

Requiring “Hey Siri” can help prevent accidental activations.

You’ll still be able to bring up Siri with your voice, but the extra word makes it less likely to wake up when you aren’t talking to it directly.

This isn’t exclusive to iOS 27, but it’s been annoying me more recently, so thought I would throw it in here, especially with Siri AI being the prominent feature on this upgrade.

iOS 27 now automatically reveals subtitles on videos in Photos, Safari and other apps that use Apple’s video player. I don’t mind captions when I need them, but they can take up too much of the video and distract me from whatever I’m watching.

They don’t appear randomly though. By default, iOS can turn them on when the video is in another language, when your iPhone is muted or when you skip back.

Whenever subtitles appear in Apple’s video player, you can tap the video to show the playback controls, tap the More Controls button, select Subtitles and choose Off.

You can disable subtitles per video.

If iOS keeps turning them on because it thinks the video is in another language, go to Settings > Accessibility > Subtitles & Captioning. Under Automatic Subtitles, turn off When Languages Don’t Match.

The same menu also has switches for Show When Muted and Show on Skip Back, so you can disable those behaviors individually without turning off every automatic subtitle feature.

You can also disable each automatic subtitle trigger individually.

Some apps and websites use their own video players, so you may need to find a separate CC or subtitles button instead.

For more on iOS 27, check out this article on the features it brings to your iPhone and how Siri AI helped one of my colleagues avoid eating diarrhea lettuce.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Vulcan rocket fails during launch, dealing major blow to SpaceX competitors

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry.
  • The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military’s national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan rolls out booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink.
  • Vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry.

The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military’s national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan rolls out booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink. Sunday’s failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time.

Vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights. In each case, the rocket corrected for those problems and continued into orbit to deploy its payloads. The incidents trigged months-long reviews and investigations before ULA could resume Vulcan flights.

Sources indicate that sunday’s launch succumbed to a different kind of failure. The six solid rocket boosters appeared to perform well in the first two minutes after Vulcan’s liftoff from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, at 12:40 pm EDT (17:40 UTC).

In a statement, ULA said the rocket “suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.” The company said it did not immediately have “any specific data to understand what occurred.”.

In a recent development, “ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us,” the firm said in a statement. “That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard.”.

Engineers will investigate the failure to “find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as swiftly as possible,” ULA mentioned.

“ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action. We will provide further updates when new information becomes available.”.

The first indications of trouble Sunday appeared to crop up before the 10-minute mark of the flight, the point in time when ULA initially said the anomaly occurred.

Multiple sources told Ars the anomaly that impacted the launch occurred in the booster stage of the rocket, not the Centaur V upper stage or the solid rocket boosters. It could not immediately be determined whether the booster stage issue was caused by the two methane-burning BE-4 engines that power it, some other part of the booster that feeds propellant into the engines, or another problem.

Heading northeast from Cape Canaveral, Vulcan jettisoned its spent solid rocket boosters on time, leaving the launcher flying on the power of its twin BE-4 main engines supplied by Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’s space tech giant. The BE-4s, each designed to produce more than a half-million pounds of thrust, were supposed to shut down just shy of the flight’s five-minute mark. However, they continued firing for at least 30 additional seconds.

Such an overburn could be an indication the booster stage was not performing as expected and operated longer to try to compensate for the underperformance.

Sources indicate that A mission animation on ULA’s broadcast, driven by real-time telemetry data from the rocket, showed Vulcan start to spin moments after booster engine shutdown. The spin continued through separation of the rocket’s Centaur V upper stage a few seconds later. ULA’s launch commentator confirmed ignition of the Centaur’s two RL10 engines, and the animation showed them vectoring thrust in an apparent attempt to put the rocket back on course.

ULA ended its live broadcast a few minutes later without discussion of the anomaly. The firm then released a statement on social media declaring the launch a failure. This was the first total mission failure for United Launch Alliance since its formation in 2006 with the merger of the rocket divisions of Boeing and Lockheed Martin.

Sunday’s incident is bad news for ULA’s two primary customers: Amazon and the US Space Force. It’s also a potential setback for NASA’s Artemis program to return astronauts to the Moon.

First, Amazon. The loss of 40 Amazon Leo satellites onboard the Vulcan rocket is, by itself, a secondary concern next to the inevitable grounding of the organization’s primary launch provider. Amazon has 37 more Vulcan rolls out reserved with ULA, each of which is slated to deliver 40 or more Amazon Leo satellites to orbit.

Sources indicate that the Amazon Leo constellation today consists of 396 satellites, a fraction of the network’s planned total of 3,292 first-generation spacecraft. Amazon officials told Ars in October that the company has enough satellites to start initial commercial Internet service by the end of the year, but more debuts are required to realize the network’s full capacity.

Amazon is setting up its service as the first head-to-head competitor in the consumer satellite broadband market with the Starlink network owned by Elon Musk and SpaceX. OneWeb and other companies also offer Internet connectivity from space, but their business models focus on beaming capacity to traditional telco providers, not directly to consumers.

Previous delays with the Vulcan rocket have kept Amazon satellites on the ground far longer than the firm planned. Amazon recently announced it manufactured its 1,000th satellite, meaning more than half of its network nodes are sitting in storage. Finally, Amazon was looking forward to ramping up its launch cadence, with Sunday’s launch the first for Amazon Leo on ULA’s Vulcan rocket.

In a recent development, “There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01,” Amazon remarked in a statement. “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”.

Amazon made launch bookings with Europe’s Arianespace and Bezos’s Blue Origin at the same time it signed the contract for 38 Vulcan introduces in 2022. Amazon reserved additional launches with Arianespace in September, bringing that company’s total contract to 24 launches for Amazon. Three have launched so far, and the fourth is set to take off later this month on an Ariane 6 rocket from French Guiana.

Sources indicate that blue Origin’s Newly introduced Glenn rocket has also encountered setbacks on its early missions. Most recently, a New Glenn rocket exploded during a ground test in Florida in May, knocking Blue Origin’s launch pad offline until at least the end of this year. The New Glenn that exploded was supposed to launch a batch of Amazon Leo satellites, but luckily for Amazon, the payloads were not stacked aboard the rocket at the time.

Sources indicate that what’s more, the Newly introduced Glenn rocket uses a version of the BE-4 engine similar to the one that flies on ULA’s Vulcan rocket. Investigators traced the New Glenn explosion to a faulty valve on one of the booster’s BE-4 engines. If engineers determine a BE-4 was at fault on Sunday’s Vulcan failure, it could stand in the way of Blue Origin returning New Glenn to flight early next year.

In a recent development, that would mean more delays for two of the rockets Amazon needs to get its satellites in orbit. Amazon’s past rocket woes forced officials to contract with SpaceX, Bezos’s chief competitor in the satellite broadband and launch sectors, to use its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket to speed up Amazon Leo deployment. Amazon has 10 more missions booked on SpaceX’s Falcon 9, and will presumably be unable to buy more as SpaceX moves the rocket toward retirement.

In a recent development, it’s a similar story for the Space Force, which relies upon SpaceX and ULA to launch the military’s most sensitive national security satellites. The Space Force in 2025 added Blue Origin’s Newly introduced Glenn as a third option to launch the country’s critical military payloads.

In a recent development, vulcan’s earlier delays forced Space Force officials to move six national security launches from ULA to SpaceX. Military officials used the swaps to get time-sensitive payloads into space sooner on Falcon 9 or Falcon Heavy, rather than waiting for Vulcan. In exchange, the Space Force awarded a future SpaceX mission to ULA.

According to recent reports, expect more Space Force rocket swaps after Vulcan’s errant launch Sunday. For the foreseeable future, the Pentagon will only increase its already heavy dependence on SpaceX to send US national security satellites to space as military leaders race to keep pace with China’s growing presence in orbit.

But SpaceX has made it clear Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy won’t be around much longer. Musk’s tech giant is rapidly transitioning to Starship to launch its own Starlink satellites and latest orbiting AI-powered compute platforms. SpaceX has not revealed prepares yet to certify Starship for national security missions, a process that would take multiple years.

Sources indicate that amazon will likely have to use the 10 Falcon 9 launches it has already reserved and Europe’s Ariane 6 rocket to add any more Amazon Leo satellites to the network in the coming months. Blue Origin’s Upcoming Glenn, once it returns to flight, has a series of backlogged launches for NASA’s Artemis Moon program next year, including key test flights of Blue’s lunar lander to prepare for future human missions. Those Moon lander tests could be pushed back further if the BE-4 engine was at fault for Sunday’s failure.

In a recent development, NASA’s lunar program has another key link to the Vulcan rocket. The space agency recently confirmed it selected a version of ULA’s Centaur upper stage for future flights of NASA’s Space Launch System rocket, the vehicle used for launching astronaut crews to the Moon. The Centaur will replace a more expensive, unproven Boeing upper stage design. NASA officials will want to rule out a problem with the Centaur V upper stage on Sunday’s doomed launch as the agency aims to start flying ULA’s Centaur on SLS missions for crewed lunar flights as soon as 2028.

Recent findings suggest that “Appreciate you promptly keeping the public and your partners informed,” NASA Administrator wrote in reply to ULA’s statement on the Vulcan launch anomaly. “The team at NASA is available to assist in all matters related to the investigation and remediation effort. Artemis, Moon Base, and the nation need ULA. We are in your corner and here to help.”.

Riders in Las Vegas can hail Amazon-owned Zoox’s steering-wheel-free robotaxis through the Uber app — with an MGM Resorts partnership and a 2027 Los Angeles expansion on the way.

Uber may be breaking up with Waymo, but it’s also gaining a new robotaxi BFF: Amazon. Starting today, Uber riders in Las Vegas can be matched with Amazon-owned Zoox’s purpose-built, bidirectional robotaxis.

It’s a first for both companies: the first time Uber is adding a purpose-built, steering-wheel-free autonomous vehicle to its network, and the first time that Zoox is opening up its fleet to a third-party app. Uber says that anyone ordering an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric, or Wait & Save in Sin City can get matched with a Zoox at no extra charge. Just like with Uber’s other AV partnerships (like Waymo in Phoenix and Austin, for now), riders can toggle a preference in the app’s Ride Preferences settings to boost their chances of getting an autonomous pod.

In a recent development, unlike Uber’s human drivers, Zoox has some geographic limitations. The organization’s robotaxis only cover heavy tourist zones, like the Strip, downtown Las Vegas, and the Arts District. And Zoox isn’t abandoning its standalone app; it will continue to operate independently alongside the Uber integration.

Alongside the launch, Uber and Zoox unveiled a multiyear deal making them the official rideshare and robotaxi partners for MGM Resorts International in Las Vegas. Anyone who has ever tried to catch a ride at the Bellagio or MGM Grand knows that resort pickup zones are notoriously chaotic. For autonomous vehicles, navigating sprawling, poorly mapped casino entrances — where valets, idling tour buses, and confused tourists all mill about — is a major technical headache.

Sources indicate that to keep Zoox’s pods from getting stuck in endless resort traffic loops, the partnership goes beyond simple branding. MGM, Uber, and Zoox say they are rolling out physical infrastructure tweaks, like clearer on-property wayfinding and custom in-app guidance designed to make pickups and drop-offs actually work smoothly for driverless cars.

Recent findings suggest that uber and Zoox aren’t stopping at Vegas. The two companies already have their eyes their next major market: Los Angeles. Zoox plans to launch initial standalone operations in LA through its own app before the end of 2026, followed by a full Uber integration sometime in 2027.

Uber’s playbook of welcoming a variety of small and large robotaxi players into its app came after the firm pivoted away from building its own self-driving tech. Now it’s attempting to position itself as an indispensable platform for every autonomous vehicle operator, including Motional, WeRide, Avride, and Zoox.

Recent findings suggest that of course, Uber’s strategy has had some drawbacks, too. Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana recently announced an end to her firm’s exclusive partnership with Uber in Austin and Atlanta by January 2028, calling it a “crapshoot.”.

They'll then receive non-jargony responses with links to peer-reviewed clinical sources. Apple's goal is to use the data to create AI health tools that deliver relevant, easy-to-understand and actionable health information.

Apple notes that the app is not integrated with Siri or Apple Intelligence, and stated that participant data will remain confidential and won't be used to train AI models.

In a recent development, "[We] believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding," mentioned Apple VP of Health and fitness Sumbul Desai, MD, in a statement. "Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.".

Bedrock Energy raises $24M to build more AI-enabled geothermal drill rigs for enterprise buildings

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dig deep enough, and the temperature of the ground remains steady year round, a fun trivia fact that has the potential to improve efficiency and slash costs for heating and cooling across the country.
  • Geothermal heat pumps, which use the ground as a heat source in winter and heat sink in summer, have been around for decades, but they’re underutilized.
  • In a recent development, that time savings recently helped Bedrock raise a upcoming $24 million funding round, the startup told TechCrunch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dig deep enough, and the temperature of the ground remains steady year round, a fun trivia fact that has the potential to improve efficiency and slash costs for heating and cooling across the country.

Geothermal heat pumps, which use the ground as a heat source in winter and heat sink in summer, have been around for decades, but they’re underutilized. Just a fraction of all buildings in the U.S. use them in part because it’s expensive to drill into the earth. But one startup, Bedrock Energy, says its AI-directed rigs can slash drilling times by up to 80%, significantly reducing costs.

In a recent development, that time savings recently helped Bedrock raise a upcoming $24 million funding round, the startup told TechCrunch. Previously, it raised a $12 million Series A in 2025 and an $8.5 million seed round in 2023.

Bedrock has focused mostly on commercial properties to date, since they benefit from deep, accurate boreholes which maximize the use of their small footprints. But the startup has also been talking with data center developers, Joselyn Lai, co-founder and CEO of Bedrock Energy, told TechCrunch. Some might use it for cooling server racks, but others are interested in the technology’s flat load profile — deploying it on neighboring properties can open up significant capacity on the grid.

In a recent development, “We had someone in Michigan say, if we could free up a few megawatts, I think we might be able to operate that many months or even a year earlier,” Lai remarked. “A year of revenue for a data center is very meaningful.”.

Recent findings suggest that bedrock says its modernized approach to shallow geothermal drilling — up to 1,0000 feet or so — sets it apart. Most geothermal heat pump drillers use rigs that are similar to those used for water wells. They work fine, but they’re crude instruments.

In a recent development, instead, Bedrock uses directional drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry, guiding them using its own models of the subsurface. That combination allows them to optimize drilling and placement, the firm claims, helping to ensure performance and longevity. Sensors in the boreholes help to refine those models.

The startup currently operates in Utah, Colorado, New York, Alberta, and its home state of Texas, and the new round will help the company expand into New England, New Jersey, the upper Midwest, and additional states in the West, Lai noted.

To power that expansion, Bedrock will add more rigs to its fleet to serve customers in those regions. Presently, it has drilled boreholes in nine sites, and it has secured payments from new customers in anticipation of drilling in the next year or two, she added.

Once up and running, a geothermal heat pump requires far less maintenance than traditional HVAC systems. “You only have to install it once and then it works for a very long time, which is very good for infrastructure from a financial perspective,” Lai said.

The newly introduced round was led by Clean Energy Ventures and Clearvision Ventures with participation from GVP Climate, Susquehanna Sustainable Investments, Catalytic Capital for Climate and Health by Temasek Trust, MUUS, Great Wave Ventures, Autodesk Foundation, Titanium Ventures, Energy Impact Partners, Wireframe Ventures, Elemental Impact, and SFV Capital.

Sony 27-inch Gaming Monitor with DualSense Charging Hook review: A piece of PC history
