⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s a perfectly adequate display with one unique hook.
  • In a recent development, it's an odd time for Sony to launch a PlayStation-branded gaming monitor, but hey, we'll take it.
  • At $349, the 27-inch Gaming Monitor with DualSense Charging Hook is a reasonably hot gaming accessory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s a perfectly adequate display with one unique hook.

In a recent development, it's an odd time for Sony to launch a PlayStation-branded gaming monitor, but hey, we'll take it. News broke in March that Sony would no longer bring its first-party games to PC, reversing course after a six-year run on desktops and teeing up a summer of heartbreak in the video game world. On the heels of this decision, Sony debuted the 27-inch Gaming Monitor with DualSense Charging Hook, advertising it as a desktop-geared peripheral that's compatible with PC, PS5 and a lineup of PlayStation accessories. It's sleek, it's sturdy, it has a crisp QHD display that supports VRR and HDR, and it features a buttery screen that handles glare well.

At $349, the 27-inch Gaming Monitor with DualSense Charging Hook is a reasonably hot gaming accessory. But more than anything, it feels like a vestigial remnant of Sony's abandoned intends to infiltrate the PC space.

The DualSense monitor has a 27-inch IPS display with QHD (2,560 x 1,440 pixels) resolution and a 240Hz refresh rate that supports VRR. Here we have the first sign that this thing was originally designed for PC play: The PS5 and PS5 Pro max out at 120Hz, and the monitor's 240Hz cap was included with PC play in mind.

It supports HDR on the spec sheet, but with a peak brightness of 350 nits and no advanced local dimming, you're mostly getting a broader range of colors rather than the eye-popping highlights the term might suggest. There's also a stereo speaker built into the display, and while its output is slightly tinny and lacking bass as you'd expect, it's perfectly acceptable. Put simply, this is a pretty standard gaming monitor in 2026.

In a recent development, as far as inputs go, there are two HDMI 2.1 ports, one DisplayPort 1.4, two USB-A slots, one USB-C connection and a 3.5mm audio output. They're tucked into a divot on the rear of the monitor and pointed downward, with a clever cable management hook that can be popped out from the stand's neck, keeping things as organized as possible.

Industry observers note that the monitor is compatible with PC, Mac, PS5 and PS5 Pro, plus it can hold and charge a DualSense or DualSense Edge gamepad. It also functions with the PlayStation Link adapter, which enables Sony's Pulse and Pulse Elite wireless headsets, Pulse Explore earbuds and Pulse Elevate wireless speakers (at least theoretically). The Pulse headset will hit the market this month, while the Elevate speakers were just recently delayed indefinitely, extending the last echoes of a grander desktop scheme.

It has been revealed that the DualSense charging dock swings down from behind the screen and hangs below the frame, and it's actually the star of the show. It's truly cute and also incredibly useful. Having a dedicated, out-of-the-way spot to store and charge an often-used gamepad is clutch.

It has been revealed that the DualSense monitor is a noticeable upgrade from both the 27-inch Samsung 1440p/144Hz TN display and the 24-inch Alienware 1080p/240Hz IPS display that I right now use. This improvement applies not only to gaming scenarios, but also your standard PC use cases, like working, creating, watching YouTube, scrolling Reddit and streaming Real Housewives.

Sony's marketing positions the monitor as a display for your desktop PS5, but this is an uncommon console configuration and it's one that I don't personally have set up in my home. So, I tested out the monitor the way most players will use it, as a PC peripheral that happens to hold and charge my spare DualSense. This worked out exceedingly well for my gaming habits, considering I play Overwatch on PC and PS5, and I prefer to use a DualSense for both (keyboard and mouse players, don't come for me). However, outside of this one title, I tend to use the Wolverine V3 Pro for my Steam games, and there's no place to adorably dangle any non-DualSense gamepad from Sony's latest display. This is also true for literally every other monitor, of course.

In a recent development, I plugged in a set of Creative Pebble speakers and my PC, popped my favorite DualSense Edge on the dock, clipped a Logitech camera and Elgato light to the top of the monitor, and I was good to go. The display naturally rests parallel to the stand neck and it can be tilted upward about 30 degrees, but not downward. The tilt action is fluid and it sticks in place well. Shifting the screen vertically is less enjoyable but still easy: Hold a button at the back of the neck and the monitor clicks into place at varying levels. If you want to lower it more than 21mm from the top, you have to hide the charging dock first.

There's a large sliding glass door beside my desk, providing ample opportunity to test the monitor's glare-management abilities. The DualSense display has an eggshell-like coating that eats light like it's late for dinner, and it maintains a bright, crisp image even in a sun-drenched room. Things only improve in dimmer conditions, and the monitor's 240Hz refresh rate is a dream compared with my previous cap of 144Hz. With 1440p resolution, VRR and up to 240 fps in-game, I don't find myself longing for 4K visuals while playing Overwatch or any other game. Of course, I'm not coming from a 4K monitor, so I would say that.

In a recent development, the monitor also looks great on the desk, with a wide and thin metal base, sleek cylindrical stand neck and subtle branding. Maybe my previous display was just severely unstable, but I find the DualSense monitor to be surprisingly sturdy, especially considering its minimal design. Say you share a desk with someone who has a habit of idly bouncing their legs throughout the day, intermittently shaking the entire workspace and sometimes even knocking over your aesthetically placed Sanrio figurines. (A totally random, hypothetical example, of course). The Sony Gaming Monitor holds up well to this type of abuse, wobbling just slightly even under extreme leg-bouncing conditions. It's far more stable than my previous monitor, and it doesn't make plastic creaking noises when it does sway. All told, it's a sturdy piece of equipment.

Recent findings suggest that sony's 2026 PlayStation-branded gaming monitor is sleek, clever and cute, and at $349, it's a solid investment for anyone who even occasionally uses a PlayStation controller at the desk. My final read on the dock is that it's dope: It charges and stores the DualSense in a cool way, and provides a function that no other monitor will have. Even if you don't ever pull the charging dock down, this is a capable and clean display.

Sony clearly started building the 27-inch DualSense monitor before reversing its plans to take over the PC space, so in many ways, this peripheral exists as a physical reminder of a future that will never be. You could say it's already a piece of gaming history, something that feels more ephemeral by the day.

#8. Delivery drones are coming. For some with PTSD, that's a terrifying prospect.

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1987 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Delivery drones are coming. For some with PTSD, that's a terrifying prospect.

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In August, Amazon confirmed plans to expand its Prime Air delivery drone program to “nearly 500 cities and towns by the end of 2026.” Combined with similar uncrewed aerial delivery programs from DoorDash and Zipline (in partnership with Uber and Walmart), the expansion suggests that flying robots dropping their payloads onto suburban lawns will soon be commonplace.
  • In a recent development, for many people, delivery drones will be little more than a novelty, occasionally good for a laugh when one does something ridiculous.
  • The use of all manner of weaponized drones in the ongoing war in Ukraine and in Israeli attacks on Lebanon and Gaza has already produced an epidemic of what some mental health professionals have dubbed “dronophobia.” And while relatively few US troops have been targeted by drones flown by Iran, ISIS, and Iran-backed militias throughout the Middle East, even those who have not directly been attacked may experience anxiety simply because of the ample video footage of attacks circulating in news and social media.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In August, Amazon confirmed plans to expand its Prime Air delivery drone program to “nearly 500 cities and towns by the end of 2026.” Combined with similar uncrewed aerial delivery programs from DoorDash and Zipline (in partnership with Uber and Walmart), the expansion suggests that flying robots dropping their payloads onto suburban lawns will soon be commonplace.

In a recent development, for many people, delivery drones will be little more than a novelty, occasionally good for a laugh when one does something ridiculous. For others, though, their growing use could be a nightmare. As the instant delivery industry clears the last FAA hurdles to rapid deliveries beyond an operator’s line of sight, an increasing number of people worldwide are living with post-traumatic stress disorder or other anxiety-related disorders triggered by drones.

The use of all manner of weaponized drones in the ongoing war in Ukraine and in Israeli attacks on Lebanon and Gaza has already produced an epidemic of what some mental health professionals have dubbed “dronophobia.” And while relatively few US troops have been targeted by drones flown by Iran, ISIS, and Iran-backed militias throughout the Middle East, even those who have not directly been attacked may experience anxiety simply because of the ample video footage of attacks circulating in news and social media.

Combined with broader anxiety about surveillance technologies, artificial intelligence, and things generally falling from the sky, the resulting hypervigilance could result in some unintended deliveries from those Prime Air flying robots.

Drones have been a part of the battlefield in some form since the late 1980s, when the Israeli Defense Forces began using them. From the beginning, they have had a psychological impact on both those in the sights of drone operators and the operators themselves.

The first military use of drones was for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. I witnessed the development of naval drone operations aboard USS Iowa in 1986 and 1987, and for many on the ship at the time, the drones were a curiosity—or, at worst, an annoyance. Our crews spent hours standing by a boat, ready to retrieve crashed drones from the water. But we were helping develop a capability that would eventually lead to Iraqi troops surrendering to the USS Wisconsin‘s drone during the Gulf War. Back then, drones were merely heralds of destruction, acting as forward observers for the Air Force ordnance fired or launched from elsewhere.

Iraqi troops on Faylaka Island associated the Pioneer RPV with the bombardment they had just experienced from the USS Missouri. When the Wisconsin’s drone flew in to assess the damage, their morale was broken.

Over southern Lebanon, the same kinds of drones were part of what amounted, for some residents, to sonic psychological warfare—the hum of lawnmower-like engines overhead was a reminder of constant surveillance and the ever-present threat of artillery or air strikes. The resulting anxiety intensified as drones began carrying their own weapons and “loitering munitions,” one-way drones designed to fly into targets and explode.

Israel’s continued fight against Hezbollah in Lebanon, along with the US wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, accelerated the evolution of drone warfare and expanded the population experiencing its psychological effects. A Stanford Law study in 2012 of the impact of US drones in Pakistan (PDF) highlighted how drones were destroying the fabric of communities in northwest Pakistan:.

Sources indicate that drones hover twenty-four hours a day over communities in northwest Pakistan, striking homes, vehicles, and public spaces without warning. Their presence terrorizes men, women, and children, giving rise to anxiety and psychological trauma among civilian communities. Those living under drones have to face the constant worry that a deadly strike may be fired at any moment and the knowledge that they are powerless to protect themselves.

That experience has been repeated and amplified in current conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon, and Ukraine. A team of US and Ukrainian psychiatrists has reported that Ukrainian military personnel and civilians who have experienced a drone attack, particularly those injured in one, “are at heightened risk for developing persistent psychological symptoms, a vulnerability intensified by the ongoing threat of repeated attacks.”.

Those symptoms—a “unique hypervigilance behavior with corresponding hyperarousal and avoidance behaviors”—are now referred to by some Ukrainian doctors as “dronophobia.”.

“The distinct hum of an approaching drone, often likened to the swarming of hornets, has itself become a psychological weapon,” noted the team led by Dr. Joseph L. Bonvie of Massachusetts General Hospital. “The escalating pitch as a drone draws near elicits fear and helplessness even before an attack.”.

Similar symptoms have been reported in women and children in Gaza, where Israeli drone strikes have been persistent. In consultations with 19 patients in Gaza, “all patients reported an intense phobic reaction to the acoustic signature of drones (the ‘zannana’), associated with imminent bombing and death, manifesting as full-blown panic attacks,” wrote Dr. Mohammad Abu Slaih, a Jordanian psychiatrist, in an article for European Psychiatry. “Three children developed a specific fear of looking at the sky. “.

The Iranian drone attacks on Gulf states, while hardly comparable to what Gaza has endured, have had a broad impact on civilians in the United Arab Emirates and other countries in the region, disrupting sleep, causing fatigue, and fueling anticipatory anxiety as people wait for the next drone to strike.

Recent findings suggest that that anxiety is common across populations exposed to drone warfare. The US Army Training and Doctrine Command (TRADOC) has compared drones’ potential to induce PTSD to the “shell shock” of World War I and the “battle fatigue” of World War II, noting that the “fear and stress from (the sound of) near-persistent drone presence creates anticipatory anxiety… Fears can persist beyond the drone’s presence, enhancing a soldier’s anxiety even when out of harm’s way.”.

Recent findings suggest that the use of drone video by both Russia and Ukraine as a psychological warfare tool extends the impact of drones beyond those who experience attacks firsthand. Footage of attacks on individual soldiers has been posted on social media to spread anxiety among opposing forces, sometimes going viral and exposing thousands of other people to the attacks. Ukrainian military units often publish first-person-view videos of drones chasing down Russian soldiers, complete with horror-film-styled soundtracks.

According to recent reports, according to Neda Gould, an associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, that aspect sets drone-induced PTSD apart from other types of the disorder. In an interview with Psychiatry Online, Gould stated social media could amplify trauma because “not only does the soldier have to grapple with the PTSD-related consequences of the attack itself, but they may also relive the experience in a way that is completely out of their control,” especially when social media comments express support for the attacks.

The US military has grappled with drone-induced PTSD and other mental health symptoms over the past 15 years. The first signs of stress for American troops, however, came from drone operators themselves.

In 2014, a team of researchers led by a US Air Force psychologist found that 4.3 percent of Air Force drone operators displayed “a pattern of symptoms of moderate to extreme level of severity” associated with PTSD. More recent studies have found that drone operators are just as likely to experience PTSD symptoms as members of aircrews deployed to war zones. Differences in how crews operate between manned combat aircraft and unmanned systems crews may even put drone operators at greater risk of psychological impact.

The dual psychological impact of drone warfare was aptly demonstrated by Killbox, a video artwork and “game” that presents two perspectives: those of a drone operator and a child on the ground. Playing it leaves many people deeply saddened, offering a glimpse of the moral injury some drone operators have experienced after their missions.

US troops are no longer just the ones behind the screens, however. Beginning with operations against ISIS, US troops have faced increasingly sophisticated drone warfare, starting with grenades dropped by ISIS-operated consumer quadcopter drones in 2017. Since then, Iranian-built drones, some based on reverse-engineered technology from downed US drones, have been used against US troops and ships by Iran and Iranian-backed militias in Yemen and Iraq. Among these is the Shahed, a long-range attack drone that Iran has sold in large numbers to Russia for its war on Ukraine.

The US Army TRADOC report also recognized that the psychological effects of drone attacks can reach further than those wounded in attacks, and even beyond the units that encounter them, saying:.

Drones amplify the uncertainties of war because rear areas are less secure as long-range drones extend danger zones beyond that of artillery and rockets. The feeling of nowhere being safe exacerbates anxiety even when drones are not present.

In a recent development, while little public data is available on drone-induced PTSD among US veterans, evidence suggests that drones could also affect people with PTSD stemming from other kinds of trauma. The sound of a drone, its shadow, a glimpse of one in peripheral vision, or other stimuli from drones could trigger hypervigilance because of their unexpectedness, their similarity to other triggering stimuli, or a range of other factors.

Sources indicate that even for those who have not experienced drone attacks, the presence of an uncrewed aircraft can cause anxiety. Drones purportedly operated by the Department of Homeland Security in Minneapolis earlier this year appeared to be used not just for surveillance of targets of Immigration and Customs Enforcement but also to intimidate individuals who had been tracking ICE activity.

The expanding use of drones by law enforcement organizations in the US as part of “drone first responder” programs has exposed an increasing number of Americans to drone surveillance, with over 1,000 agencies applying for FAA waivers for drone operations as of February 2026, based on data from the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Combined with news reports about drone attacks and foreign governments’ use of drones, the disquiet of drone propeller noises and blinking lights in the sky has already created a War of the Worlds level of dronophobia.

Over the past two years, several drone incidents have been linked, or suspected of being linked, to state-actor espionage, with a surge in reports in November and December of 2024. Three occurred in Southern California, including a drone flyover of Vandenberg Air Force Base as a National Reconnaissance Office payload was being loaded ont0 a SpaceX rocket. A Chinese national was charged in the case and arrested while attempting to leave the country. Other cases in the US were officially downplayed as posing no security threat.

In a recent development, in November 2024, incidents in the UK centered on multiple air bases used by the US, including incursions near RAF Fairford, the base recently allegedly targeted in a plot that the British government attributed to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Similar incursions occurred in Germany.

Sources indicate that around the same time, a rash of civilian “drone sightings” across the US emerged, particularly in New Jersey. Anxiety grew further after a Republican New Jersey congressman claimed there was an “Iranian drone mothership.” Segments of the population were ready to shoot down drones themselves.

Many of these sightings turned out to be crewed aircraft or helicopters, toy drones, or, in very few cases, authorized commercial drone flights. Former Maryland Governor Larry Hogan even reported seeing dozens of large drones above his house, only for others to quickly point out that the objects were actually the constellation Orion.

PTSD is a treatable condition, and coping strategies can help people manage triggers. But severe PTSD can be extremely debilitating, and research into the effects of drones on PTSD remains limited. It’s still unclear how well survivors of drone attacks will be able to process the fears and traumatic memories associated with drones, especially if the aircraft become a pervasive part of daily life.

I, for one, won’t be placing any Prime Air orders anytime soon.

Apple Launches New App to Study How People Use AI for Health

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Since 2019, when Apple first launched its Research app, the manufacturer has partnered with medical universities and institutions to run a range of health studies on hearing, heart health and movement, women’s health and, most recently, the Apple Health Study, which covers a wide variety of health areas.
  • On Sunday, Apple released its latest study, and it comes with its own app: the Apple Health AI Study.
  • It has been revealed that during a press briefing, Apple mentioned the study aims to understand how people interact with conversational health AI tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since 2019, when Apple first launched its Research app, the manufacturer has partnered with medical universities and institutions to run a range of health studies on hearing, heart health and movement, women’s health and, most recently, the Apple Health Study, which covers a wide variety of health areas.

On Sunday, Apple released its latest study, and it comes with its own app: the Apple Health AI Study.

It has been revealed that during a press briefing, Apple mentioned the study aims to understand how people interact with conversational health AI tools. To do so, it will examine comprehension, response quality, the drivers of user trust and everyday health actions.

The goal? To inform the responsible design of health AI experiences for both Apple and the industry and to explore how health AI might help people prepare for doctor’s visits. Key questions the study aims to address include: Do owners understand the information provided by health AI? Do they trust it? Is it helpful?

This is particularly relevant considering that one in three US adults use AI chatbots for health information.

Study data will not be used to train AI models, but it may inform Apple’s feature development.

According to recent reports, to facilitate the study, Apple is partnering with OpenEvidence, an AI platform designed specifically for doctors. It generates answers using medical information from these partners: The Upcoming England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, National Comprehensive Cancer Network, Nature and Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.

In the dedicated app, study participants can ask the AI their text-based health questions and then see answers with linked, peer-reviewed clinical citations. They can also choose to share their HealthKit data, including sleep, lab results, activity and resting heart rate, for more personalized answers.

HealthKit is Apple’s hub for health and fitness data collected on the iPhone and Apple Watch.

According to recent reports, the Apple Health AI Usage Study is open to 200,000 participants. You must be in the US and age 21 or older to participate. An Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone (iPhone 15 Pro or later) running iOS 26 or later is also required.

Sources indicate that why an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone? According to Apple, the study app requires the processing capabilities of those iPhones, and it uses on-device Apple Foundation Models that are part of Apple Intelligence. These models provide access to any large language model. For example, as part of the study, these models are used to classify question categories.

In a recent development, each participant is asked to participate for up to 12 months. During this time, they can ask questions about general health, specific symptoms, recovery from a procedure and their own uploaded health data, as examples.

In addition to a baseline survey, participants will receive monthly surveys and additional surveys specific to preparing for doctor’s visits.

Participants will also be prompted to check in with the app. For instance, if you have a paired Apple Watch, you will receive notifications to check in, along with suggested topics to explore.

If there is a complete lack of participation, a participant may potentially be removed from the study.

After downloading the Apple Health AI Study app, participants must complete a mandatory onboarding process that includes informed consent. They will also be asked to share their demographic information, such as race, age and education level, which will be used to explore how these factors may affect their preferences and communication needs. Then, they can start asking the AI questions.

In a recent development, the iPhone first processes questions using tools designed to remove details that could identify participants. They then go to a secure cloud-based study environment managed by a third-party study support contractor called UST Global, where queries are delinked from individual participant IDs and screened using tools designed to further remove any remaining personal details. Lastly, this info is sent to OpenEvidence, where answers are generated using supporting reference materials.

OpenEvidence will delete both question and response data within 24 hours.

A small group of Apple researchers will have access to coded versions of survey responses, separated from personally identifiable information, summaries of conversations and categories of the most common conversation types.

Within the study app, there are also safety guardrails that detect concerning questions and respond by suggesting that a participant follow up with a provider or other resources if needed.

There is no live monitoring, and study staff won’t contact participants if any questions related to self-harm are asked.

It’s also up to the participant whether they share any HealthKit metrics. They will first have to choose to upload their clinical health records to Apple’s Health app, and then separately choose to share those records from the Health app to the fresh Apple Health AI Study app.

The Apple Health AI Study app is now available in the App Store. As of now, there is no set publication date for the study.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, congress is lining up behind bipartisan AI chip curbs aimed at China.
  • Bloomberg reported on Sunday that the bill, which also covers chipmaking equipment, could pass within weeks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Howard Lutnick in the Oval Office at his swearing-in as US commerce secretary on 21 February 2025.

In a recent development, congress is lining up behind bipartisan AI chip curbs aimed at China. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says it is not needed. And Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, the official many lawmakers blame for weak enforcement, is set to fly to China with Donald Trump this week.

Bloomberg reported on Sunday that the bill, which also covers chipmaking equipment, could pass within weeks. Lutnick is expected on Air Force One for Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping at the APEC summit, Semafor reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

It has been revealed that “I don’t think we need the legislation. We have all the rules we need. We just need them enforced,” Bessent said on Fox News’s Sunday Morning Futures.

Recent findings suggest that bessent also mentioned Nvidia needs a “dramatic shakeup”. Its board should go outside the tech giant for its next chief executive, he said, as Reuters reported. He wants answers from the board and its outside counsel within 10 days. His question is whether Nvidia ignored warning signs of shell companies funnelling chips to China. Allies of Jensen Huang are meanwhile discussing his return.

In a recent development, pressure on Lutnick grew on Sunday with a New York Times investigation by Ana Swanson, Aaron Krolik and Paul Mozur. Lutnick ran Cantor Fitzgerald for decades before handing it to his sons. The Times found that Cantor has worked with Southeast Asian data centre companies that serve Chinese clients.

It has been revealed that one is Bitdeer, a Singaporean firm building a data centre called A201 in Malaysia’s Johor state. Cantor acted as a sales agent for Bitdeer’s equity offering of up to $1bn this year. A person with knowledge of the arrangement told the Times the site will likely serve Tencent. Renting chips this way is legal, and it sidesteps the ban on selling advanced chips directly to Chinese firms.

Lutnick is writing the rules that would decide whether that route stays open. Commerce has pushed for a narrower version than others in the administration wanted, people familiar with the talks told the Times. The Times found no evidence that Cantor’s investments influenced him. A Commerce spokeswoman said he acts in the best interests of the United States. He does not discuss department matters with his sons, she added.

On Sunday, the Wall Street Journal reported how Huang built this route. It said the Southeast Asian data centres gave Chinese companies computing power and cover for alleged chip smuggling.

In January, Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter told more than a dozen officials what Trump wanted on licence conditions for H200 exports to China, Semafor reported on Friday. People with access to an account of the call gave Semafor his words.

Recent findings suggest that “I was with the president when he and Jensen discussed this so I want to let you know what the president wanted. He wants this to go fast,” Teter said, according to Semafor.

It has been revealed that nvidia called a rule that sellers know their cloud customers a “poison pill”, Semafor reported. It also pushed to raise the threshold for buyer checks to tens of thousands of chips. A Bureau of Industry and Security spokesperson told Semafor such talks with companies are “completely routine”. Nvidia declined to comment. Commerce had already halted its Megaspeed probe after Teter contacted a senior official, the Times reported earlier this month.

“It looks like he has been the barrier inside the government to stopping the flow of these Nvidia chips to China. And the question is why?” Representative Jim Himes said on CBS’s Face the Nation.

Republican John Moolenaar, who chairs the House China committee, noted Lutnick and the whole Commerce Department need to answer questions. Democrats, who take control of Congress in January, strategy to ask why Lutnick declined to blacklist suspected smugglers, Representative Stephen Lynch told The Washington Post.

Sources indicate that senator Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, wrote to Lutnick on Sunday ahead of the Xi meeting, CNBC reported. She urged him to enforce export controls under the 2018 Export Control Reform Act and stop chips reaching barred companies.

“These failures to carry out the law help give away America’s technology advantage in AI,” Cantwell wrote.

Cantwell also pointed to Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2bn in Nvidia stock when Lutnick was nominated. She said the administration’s 25% fee on some Nvidia chip sales to China could create a financial incentive to approve exports. Commerce did not immediately respond to CNBC.

The Post also reported, citing a former administration official, that Bessent confronted Lutnick over why he had not acted despite instructions from Trump on three occasions. Bessent has said publicly that Commerce has the pen. Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on 10 December.

The White House notes it has complete confidence in Lutnick, according to Semafor. A senior US official told reporters the Nvidia scandal should have no bearing on the China trip.

Industry News: How to use your phone to find an Apple TV remote

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that lost in the cushions again?
  • In a recent development, is there anyone in the world who owns a TV and hasn't lost the remote at least once?
  • Apple has a dedicated Remote app that will let you locate the device much like you'd use an AirTag.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that lost in the cushions again? Here is how to find your remote without buying a new one.

In a recent development, is there anyone in the world who owns a TV and hasn't lost the remote at least once? Unlikely, right? Now that remotes are slimmer and more compact, it's an even more prevalent occurrence. Losing your Apple TV remote is just as easy, of course. It can slip between couch cushions, end up under the blankets or get left somewhere when someone gets up from the couch to grab some water. The good news, however, is that your smartphone can actually help you find your Apple TV remote anywhere in your home.

Apple has a dedicated Remote app that will let you locate the device much like you'd use an AirTag. To find a missing Apple TV remote, you just have to pop open the app and hunt for the "Locate Remote" button, which will then trigger a beeping sound from the remote itself if you have the 2026 Apple TV 4K model. That helps if the thing's buried under the cushions.

It has been revealed that in the meantime, you could also use that same Remote app to turn your phone into a fully functional Apple TV controller. Android consumers have some workarounds too. As long as your phone is connected to the same Wi-Fi network as your Apple TV, you can regain control within minutes. You just have to know how.

According to recent reports, if you've dug through the couch cushions, turned over every blanket, looked under the sofa and checked your kid's toy bins and still haven't found the remote, it's time to bring out the massive guns. And by big guns, we mean to launch the Apple TV Remote app. This tool requires an iPhone running iOS 17 or later, while the Apple TV must have tvOS 17 or later. You have to open the Control Center on your iPhone and then tap on the Apple TV Remote. From there, tap the device list, tap Find and follow the prompts on your iPhone to locate your remote. The onscreen circle grows and grows and the text changes from far to near to here in a techy game of Hot and Cold.

The new Siri Remote that Apple released with its refreshed Apple TV 4K in October 2026 has Precision Finding hardware, which means it's easier to find with onscreen directional arrows and live distance guidance. There's even a built-in speaker that plays a chime to locate it. Previous models only come with proximity searching, so you'll have to rely on your phone to find the remote.

In case your remote is nowhere to be found and not even the built-in location feature is of help, then you have to try out a different method. You could, of course, order a newly introduced remote, but that's not absolutely necessary, and a new Apple TV is supposed to last long enough that losing a remote shouldn't push you to replace the whole setup.

To use the Apple TV remote, you just need to access your iPhone's or iPad's Control Center. As we already discussed, you have to tap on the Apple TV Remote button and then on your Apple TV or smart TV that's AirPlay-compatible from the list. You might need to enter a four-digit passcode to confirm the connection.

Once that's set up, you can use your phone as a TV remote to do things like control volume, open and close the device, switch streaming apps, control playback and so on. Everything you can do with the actual, physical Apple Remote, you can do with this app.

If you're an Android user, there's no official Apple-made remote app to use. There are, however, workarounds to replace your lost Apple TV remote without spending money. Third-party apps like Remote for Apple TV are available on the Google Play Store and replicate the core remote functionality of the physical remote. You'll need to download the app, ensure your Android phone is connected to the same Wi-Fi network as the Apple TV and type in the onscreen code for pairing. Then you use the digital remote to hunt for your next binge-worthy show.

See? Losing the Apple TV remote doesn't have to derail your viewing session. The Remote app is the fastest and most reliable solution whenever you can't find the remote and you really want to turn down the volume or swap the app. Once you can hear your own thoughts again, you can resume your search for the device.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jensen Huang’s absence has left the AI industry in limbo.﻿.
  • Jensen Huang’s absence has left the AI industry in limbo.﻿.
  • In a recent development, for years, Jensen Huang has had an almost unprecedented power to shape AI’s advancement as Nvidia’s CEO, cofounder, and president.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang’s absence has left the AI industry in limbo.﻿.

Jensen Huang’s absence has left the AI industry in limbo.﻿.

In a recent development, for years, Jensen Huang has had an almost unprecedented power to shape AI’s advancement as Nvidia’s CEO, cofounder, and president. As The Verge wrote last week, Nvidia’s chips are “the bedrock upon which advanced AI technology in the US is being built.” Ever-increasing demand has consistently outpaced supply, leading AI CEOs to essentially bow at Huang’s feet as they vie for more compute ahead of their much-hyped IPOs. Nvidia also has a varied investment portfolio of up-and-coming AI companies from neoclouds to infrastructure firms, worth nearly $100 billion, and Huang has President Donald Trump’s ear. He’s even been called Trump’s “most influential adviser” when it comes to technology. As of last Wednesday, however, Huang — a pivotal figure in the industry — is no longer CEO of Nvidia.

Sources indicate that since Huang’s resignation last week, the scandal over his multiple affairs has shown no sign of waning. After the announcement, Nvidia shares dropped 14 percent, making it one of the worst weeks on the market for the firm in the past year and a half. And the revelations kept coming. Hours after the resignation, Reuters reported that Huang had had a third affair with a second employee (though the employee was unnamed). We learned that Huang had reportedly misled Nvidia leaders about his infidelity, that Nvidia was allegedly linked to the supply of nearly $12 billion of its chips to China, and that alleged Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang’s companies reportedly promised advanced chips to Chinese AI company DeepSeek.

According to recent reports, there’s reportedly been a petition to bring back Huang by some Nvidia employees, as well as reports of Huang assembling a “war room” of allies to float a comeback as Nvidia CEO. Lawmakers have begun investigations into the alleged chip-smuggling and other offenses. Every day, there’s increasing evidence of fallout inside the Trump administration. And as Nvidia’s quarterly earnings on Tuesday loom, the future of the manufacturer and the AI industry as a whole remain in flux.

According to recent reports, what does an Nvidia without Huang look like? It’s hard to say, since he’s been at the helm for 33 years. CFO Colette Kress has taken on the role of interim CEO, and the broader AI world is waiting to see where one of the world’s most valuable companies — and one that helped shape the industry’s every milestone — goes from here.

Sources indicate that nvidia is such a large manufacturer that the implications of Huang’s departure “will take years to play out,” remarked Stephen Straus, CEO of KUNGFU.AI, an AI consulting firm. “[Nvidia has] their market share … they have the world’s best chips, they have the most manufacturing capacity … and they have a whole ecosystem built around what they’ve done. None of that changes with one person.” While there’s been discussion of Huang’s departure speeding along an AI bubble burst, Straus compares the situation to the dot-com bust — which didn’t stop the growth of the internet itself.

It has been revealed that huang’s resignation may not cause a domino effect in AI, but longer-term AI funding initiatives championed by him may eventually be affected, says Lior Prosor, managing partner at Deep33, a tech VC firm. Huang championed fundraising for the broader AI buildout: In August, Nvidia signed deals with six large financial institutions for about $500 billion to fund AI infrastructure expansion, and those agreements or future ones could look different if “the most prominent CEO in the AI landscape is no longer orchestrating such deals,” wrote Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello in a note last week on Monday.

Some lawmakers were already planning to pull CEOs before Congress.

Far downstream of the biggest companies, smaller AI startups are wondering how the effects will trickle down. Michal Miernowski, co-founder and CEO of Amperos Health, which builds AI agents for healthcare billing, sits in the applied AI space about two layers removed from Nvidia. He doesn’t anticipate Amperos being directly affected much by the moves, since it relies on a mix of frontier AI models and open-source ones, but a cooling of the larger AI market — whether due to the Nvidia scandal or broader concerns — could stall business as well. There’s also more to come on Nvidia’s side, from the organization’s investigation into Huang’s actions to Congressional inquiries. Evan Gotlob, partner at DarrowEverett LLP and a former state and federal prosecutor, mentioned he thinks “there’s definitely more” to the story about potential leaks to China and suspicious chip dealing. He added the board’s investigation would “obviously” continue despite his departure: “The investigation is really not going to turn out anything good for him.”.

Industry observers note that some new lawmakers already planned to haul CEOs to Capitol Hill to testify under oath. The AI populism movement is growing, as well as the blowback against data centers, which was a key talking point in Democrats’ campaigns during the midterms. The revelations around Huang, a major Trump ally, provide an early opportunity to take action.

“We want to see a Democratic Congress investigate Nvidia for anti-competitive practices that pass off costs to consumers, what the manufacturer knew about chip smuggling operations with China, and what Nvidia received in exchange for donations to the Trump campaign and ballroom,” Sacha Haworth, founder and CEO of The Tech Oversight Project, told The Verge.

According to recent reports, AI safety researchers also worry that in the worst-case scenario, the instability around last week’s events could speed up potentially dangerous AI milestones like recursive self-improvement, i.e., powerful AI that can autonomously improve and build future versions of itself. Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, an AI safety firm and third-party auditor, noted he worries that the volatility stemming from Huang’s departure “actually increases loss of control risk because companies feel even more revenue pressure and therefore are more willing to cut corners on safety.”.

In a recent development, early last week, before Huang’s resignation, the general consensus among Silicon Valley heavyweights, analysts, and politicians was that Huang’s “irreplaceable” impact would mean a return to the status quo for Nvidia. Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello wrote in a note that day that the firm “can’t rule out … Nvidia returning to business as usual” since Huang is the “only CEO the organization has ever known.” Now, as Huang reportedly assembles allies to push for a comeback the likes of which haven’t been seen since the 2023 Sam Altman coup, the entire AI industry is waiting to see which way it will go.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s never been easy to run a battery startup in the U.S.
  • Sources indicate that not all of them die, though.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s never been easy to run a battery startup in the U.S. There have been more failures than successes over the last 20 years, and whipsawing federal policy has caused more than a few battery companies to shut shop.

Sources indicate that not all of them die, though. Our Next Energy (ONE) had some close calls, but soon it will go public via SPAC, the manufacturer exclusively told TechCrunch.

ONE says it is valued at $600 million pre-money, and it expects the merger with Wen Acquisition Corp. will bring $400 million in gross proceeds assuming no redemptions. The combined tech giant will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ONEE”, and the pro forma implied equity value is $1 billion.

Over the years, ONE has raised $483 million, according to PitchBook, and at one point was valued at $1.3 billion. It has also received tens of millions of dollars in incentives tied to investments and job creation in Michigan.

Recent findings suggest that ONE is the brainchild of former Ford and Apple engineer Mujeeb Ijaz, who designed a way for electric vehicles to draw power from two batteries of different chemistries. In ONE’s first setup, it paired lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) and with a manganese-rich chemistry, which would let each chemistry play to its strengths: LFP could be used day in, day out, while the more fragile but energy-dense, manganese-rich one would work for long, infrequent road trips. An initial prototype traveled over 600 miles on a single charge.

In a recent development, but the EV market didn’t take off as promptly as anticipated, and automakers wanted to buy at lower prices (usually from China). Both of those reasons helped sink ONE’s first attempt at a Series C in late 2023. The startup had to lay off a chunk of its staff, and eventually vacated its lease for a planned $1.6 billion factory in Michigan.

It has been revealed that the rough patch led to Ijaz’s ouster as CEO in December 2023, only to have him return to the position in March 2025 after a fresh round of funding closed. (His brother’s investment firm co-led the round.).

Part of the critique aimed at ONE during Ijaz’s first tenure as CEO was that the firm spent too much time developing latest products instead of focusing on one or two, as most startups tend to do. When Ijaz came back to the helm last year, he mentioned that ONE would leave the automotive market and focus on grid-scale batteries.

Recent findings suggest that ONE isn’t alone in pivoting away from vehicle batteries. American automakers, which had similarly rosy views of EV adoption, also bet significant on battery factories and supply chains. When sales didn’t pop in the U.S. like they have in China or Europe, they had to find an outlet for that capacity, and the grid started looking like the obvious target once it started groaning under the weight of AI data centers. Both Ford and GM have announced their own energy storage products.

It has been revealed that many latest grid-scale batteries use LFP, which is safer and cheaper than those used in most EVs in the U.S., and Ijaz saw an opportunity for ONE there as well. “We go back to the origins of LFP in this country and even to some of the factories that are in China,” he remarked. Indeed, just over a decade ago Ijaz led the automotive division at A123 Systems, the manufacturer that first commercialized the chemistry.

Soon, Ijaz saw other opportunities for ONE’s batteries, including defense and locomotives.

In a recent development, the defense play isn’t surprising. Nearly every battery tech giant I talk with these days mentions defense, in part because it’s a market that Chinese companies can’t play in. Building an American supply chain means that a company can sell batteries at a premium, shielded as they are from Chinese competition. It’s a higher-margin market, though much smaller than EVs.

My recent conversation with Ijaz last week was the first time I’d heard a firm pitch rail companies as potential customers, though. Ijaz noted ONE is “finding a lot of traction in” that market. The company has built a hybrid locomotive that uses a 2.8 megawatt-hour battery, and another he calls a micro-hybrid, which uses a smaller battery to start the diesel engine faster, similar to a stop-start system on a fossil fuel car or truck.

“Our customers are seeing a 50% improvement in diesel fuel consumption, which is a big deal,” Ijaz said.

Currently, ONE has three business lines, which could be a sign of its old culture creeping back into the picture. But Ijaz noted the addition of defense and rail were driven by the bottom line: Grid-scale battery customers are also “very much like automotive customers, where they were willing to buy from China as long as the price was low enough,” he said.

“Believe me, I would have loved to have made that grid business into the single business of the company. But the customers would look and then be taken away to a Chinese option because of the pricing, and the tariffs also leading them to that conclusion,” Ijaz said. “And so we decided that we needed a more durable market, and we looked for who in the customer base valued an American battery company.”.

In a recent development, today, ONE operates a pack assembly plant in Novi, Michigan, which can put together packs from cells at a rate of 3 gigawatt-hours per year. The plant uses cells from China-based and non-China-based suppliers, as well as ONE’s own cells from a smaller factory nearby, which is currently being upgraded to make 50 megawatt-hours of batteries per year.

In its investor pitch, which TechCrunch has reviewed, ONE distills its business lines into defense and rail. Drones and submarines make up the majority of what ONE sees as a $16.2 billion market. Defense-focused data centers get lumped in there, too, contributing $4.1 billion to the defense business. (That appears to be the main outlet for grid-scale batteries.) The other line, which serves the rail industry, is expected to be worth $28.2 billion.

Both markets are sizable, but they pale in comparison to the EV sector, which is worth about $73 billion today, and could grow to $200 billion by the end of the decade, according to Grand View Research. This year, ONE expects to bring in $30 million in revenue, and hopes to make double that next year. The company said it has $200 million in binding, multi-year contracts with railroads and defense contractors.

According to recent reports, ONE hasn’t closed the door on the automotive industry, Ijaz said. “Automotive still is a race to the bottom on margins,” he said. “As time goes on, if we win an automotive contract for any purpose, we’ll take a look at it, but not at any cost.”.

Recent findings suggest that ONE’s pitch centers on the so-called foreign entity of concern (FEOC) restrictions: The U.S. government can’t buy batteries made in China or those made using minerals from China-controlled supply chains, so ONE will target them first.

But it’s a pitch that many battery companies are making today. Whether investors buy into ONE’s vision will depend on if they think the firm has parted with its tumultuous past and found a focus. It will need both to succeed in the increasingly cutthroat battery industry.
